Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $v_1,\dots,v_n\in V$ be linearly independent vectors in a $k$-vector space $V$ and let $w_1,\dots,w_n\in W$ satisfy $\sum_{i=1}^n v_i\otimes w_i=0$ in $V\otimes W$. Then $w_i=0$ for every $i$; equivalently, the linear map $W^n\to V\otimes W$, $(w_i)\mapsto\sum_iv_i\otimes w_i$, is injective.

If $V$ is finite-dimensional the same conclusion is proved without the Axiom of Choice.

Fix the following conventions, used on this page and by the later Hopf and Hecke pages.

- $k$ is a field ([[def-field]]) and every vector space is a $k$-vector space ([[def-vector-space]]); $\otimes$ means $\otimes_k$.
- $V\otimes W$ is the tensor product of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]], with the $k$-vector-space structure of [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and unit and universal property as in [[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]]. Every element of $V\otimes W$ is a finite sum of elementary tensors $v\otimes w$.
- Tensor powers are left-associated: $V^{\otimes 0}:=k$, $V^{\otimes 1}:=V$ and $V^{\otimes n}:=(V^{\otimes(n-1)})\otimes V$ for $n\ge2$. The empty tensor $k$ is identified with the tensor unit through the isomorphisms of [[thm-unit-isomorphisms-for-module-tensor-products]].
- For an algebra $A$ over a commutative ring ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) the opposite algebra $A^{\mathrm{op}}$ has the same underlying set and structure map and product $a\cdot b:=ba$ ([[def-opposite-ring]]).
- Finite sums $\sum_{i\in I}x_i$ follow [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]; an empty sum is $0$.

Parentheses in iterated tensor products may be dropped only after [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]] has been proved.

Let $k$ be a field and let $L,M,N,X$ be $k$-vector spaces. Write $\alpha_{A,B,C}:(A\otimes B)\otimes C\to A\otimes(B\otimes C)$ for the associators of [[thm-symmetry-and-associativity-over-a-commutative-ring]], $\sigma_{A,B}$ for its symmetries, and $\lambda,\rho$ for the unit isomorphisms of [[thm-unit-isomorphisms-for-module-tensor-products]].

1. **Naturality.** $\alpha$ and $\sigma$ are natural in all variables: for linear maps the usual squares commute; the unit isomorphisms are natural as well.
2. **Pentagon.** $(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\alpha_{M,N,X})\circ\alpha_{L,M\otimes N,X}\circ(\alpha_{L,M,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_X)=\alpha_{L,M,N\otimes X}\circ\alpha_{L\otimes M,N,X}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\otimes X\to L\otimes(M\otimes(N\otimes X))$.
3. **Unit triangle.** $(\mathrm{id}_M\otimes\lambda_N)\circ\alpha_{M,k,N}=\rho_M\otimes\mathrm{id}_N$ as maps $(M\otimes k)\otimes N\to M\otimes N$.
4. **First symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha_{L,N,M}\circ(\sigma_{N,L}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}=(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})\circ\alpha_{L,M,N}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\to L\otimes(N\otimes M)$.
5. **Second symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,M,N}=(\sigma_{L,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,N,M}\circ(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})$ as maps $L\otimes(M\otimes N)\to(N\otimes L)\otimes M$.

All five identities are equalities of $k$-linear maps between iterated tensor products.

Let $k$ be a field and let $L,M,N,X$ be $k$-vector spaces. Write $\alpha_{A,B,C}:(A\otimes B)\otimes C\to A\otimes(B\otimes C)$ for the associators of [[thm-symmetry-and-associativity-over-a-commutative-ring]], $\sigma_{A,B}$ for its symmetries, and $\lambda,\rho$ for the unit isomorphisms of [[thm-unit-isomorphisms-for-module-tensor-products]].

1. **Naturality.** $\alpha$ and $\sigma$ are natural in all variables: for linear maps the usual squares commute; the unit isomorphisms are natural as well.
2. **Pentagon.** $(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\alpha_{M,N,X})\circ\alpha_{L,M\otimes N,X}\circ(\alpha_{L,M,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_X)=\alpha_{L,M,N\otimes X}\circ\alpha_{L\otimes M,N,X}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\otimes X\to L\otimes(M\otimes(N\otimes X))$.
3. **Unit triangle.** $(\mathrm{id}_M\otimes\lambda_N)\circ\alpha_{M,k,N}=\rho_M\otimes\mathrm{id}_N$ as maps $(M\otimes k)\otimes N\to M\otimes N$.
4. **First symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha_{L,N,M}\circ(\sigma_{N,L}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}=(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})\circ\alpha_{L,M,N}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\to L\otimes(N\otimes M)$.
5. **Second symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,M,N}=(\sigma_{L,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,N,M}\circ(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})$ as maps $L\otimes(M\otimes N)\to(N\otimes L)\otimes M$.

All five identities are equalities of $k$-linear maps between iterated tensor products.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice**, through
[[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]] and
[[cor-every-vector-space-has-a-basis]]. Let $V$ be a vector space over a field
$F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and let $U$ be a linear subspace of $V$
([[def-linear-subspace]]). Then there is a linear subspace $W$ of $V$ with

$$V \;=\; U \oplus W$$

([[def-internal-direct-sum]]), that is $U + W = V$ and $U \cap W = \{0_V\}$.

No finiteness of $V$, of $U$ or of any basis is assumed.

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a
scalar action $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, satisfying

$$r(m+n)=rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m=rm+sm,\quad (rs)m=r(sm),\quad 1_Rm=m.$$

A **right $R$-module** has an action $M\times R\to M$, $(m,r)\mapsto mr$, with
the analogous right-handed axioms. Unless “right” is stated, **module** means a
unital left module.

Let $S \subseteq V$. The set of linear subspaces of $V$ containing $S$ is
nonempty, since $V$ itself is one, so its intersection is a linear subspace of
$V$ by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]]. That intersection is the **span
of $S$**,

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;:=\; \bigcap \{\, W \;:\; W \text{ is a linear subspace of } V \text{ and } S \subseteq W \,\} .$$

It contains $S$, being an intersection of sets each of which contains $S$, and it
is contained in every linear subspace of $V$ that contains $S$. So it is the
**smallest** linear subspace of $V$ containing $S$, and those two properties
determine it uniquely: if $W$ and $W'$ both contain $S$ and are each contained in
every linear subspace containing $S$, then each is contained in the other. This
is what licenses the definite article.

A subset $S \subseteq V$ **spans** $V$, or is a **spanning set** of $V$, when
$\operatorname{span}(S) = V$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). An **$R$-algebra** is a unital ring $A$ together with a unital ring homomorphism

$$\eta_A:R\longrightarrow A$$

([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) whose image is central: $\eta_A(r)a=a\eta_A(r)$ for every $r\in R$ and $a\in A$. The induced scalar action is $ra:=\eta_A(r)a$, making $A$ an $R$-module and multiplication $A\times A\to A$ bilinear.

An **$R$-algebra homomorphism** $f:A\to B$ is a unital ring homomorphism satisfying $f\circ\eta_A=\eta_B$. Such a map is automatically $R$-linear. An $R$-algebra is **commutative** when its underlying ring is commutative.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $k$, and let $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ be a finite list spanning a subspace $W$. Some sublist of $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ is a basis of $W$. In particular, a subspace spanned by a finite list is finite-dimensional. No choice principle is used.

Let $V$ be a vector space over $F$. A **linear functional** on $V$ is a linear map $f:V\to F$, where $F$ is regarded as a vector space over itself. The **algebraic dual space** of $V$ is

$$V^*:=\mathcal L(V,F),$$

with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. This is the full algebraic dual: no topology, norm, or continuity condition is imposed.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a
scalar action $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, satisfying

$$r(m+n)=rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m=rm+sm,\quad (rs)m=r(sm),\quad 1_Rm=m.$$

A **right $R$-module** has an action $M\times R\to M$, $(m,r)\mapsto mr$, with
the analogous right-handed axioms. Unless “right” is stated, **module** means a
unital left module.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). An **$R$-algebra** is a unital ring $A$ together with a unital ring homomorphism

$$\eta_A:R\longrightarrow A$$

([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) whose image is central: $\eta_A(r)a=a\eta_A(r)$ for every $r\in R$ and $a\in A$. The induced scalar action is $ra:=\eta_A(r)a$, making $A$ an $R$-module and multiplication $A\times A\to A$ bilinear.

An **$R$-algebra homomorphism** $f:A\to B$ is a unital ring homomorphism satisfying $f\circ\eta_A=\eta_B$. Such a map is automatically $R$-linear. An $R$-algebra is **commutative** when its underlying ring is commutative.

value: For every $m$, the existing tensor $\rho(m)\in M\otimes C$ represents the entire orbit because $(\operatorname{id}\otimes f)\rho(m)=f\cdot m$ for every $f$. This proves rationality without AC. If $t,t'\in M\otimes C$ both represent that orbit, then $(\operatorname{id}\otimes f)(t-t')=0$ for all $f\in C^*$, where $C^*$ is the full algebraic dual [F7]; [A1] and [F4] imply $t=t'$.

For every $m$, the existing tensor $\rho(m)\in M\otimes C$ represents the entire orbit because $(\operatorname{id}\otimes f)\rho(m)=f\cdot m$ for every $f$. This proves rationality without AC. To establish the separation used below, first assume [A1] and let $X$ be any vector space and $T\in X\otimes C$. Write $T=\sum_s x_s\otimes d_s$ as a finite tensor by [F4], and put $D=\operatorname{span}\{d_s\}$. By [F6], choose a finite ordered basis $c_1,\dots,c_q$ of $D$ and re-expand $T=\sum_i y_i\otimes c_i$. By [F5], choose a complement $E$ with $C=D\oplus E$. For each $i$, let $\lambda_i:D\to k$ be the $i$th coordinate function in the basis $c_1,\dots,c_q$, which is linear by [F9], and define $f_i(d+e)=\lambda_i(d)$ for $d\in D$ and $e\in E$. The unique direct-sum decomposition makes $f_i$ a linear functional on $C$, so $f_i\in C^*$ by [F8], and $(\operatorname{id}_X\otimes f_i)(T)=y_i$. Thus if every $f\in C^*$ annihilates $T$, every $y_i=0$ and $T=0$. If $C$ is finite-dimensional, [F6] gives a finite ordered basis $c_1,\dots,c_n$ of $C$; re-expanding $T=\sum_i y_i\otimes c_i$ and evaluating against its coordinate functionals recovers each $y_i$, so the same separation conclusion holds without [A1]. In either branch, if $t,t'\in M\otimes C$ both represent the orbit of $m$, then every $f\in C^*$ annihilates $t-t'$, and the applicable separation argument gives $t=t'$.

Now let $M$ be a rational left $C^*$-module. For each $m$ choose its representing tensor $t_m$ from [F3]; by [A1] and [F4] it is unique. Define $\rho(m):=t_m$. For $m,n$ and $a\in k$, the tensors $\rho(m+n)$ and $\rho(m)+\rho(n)$ have the same evaluation under every $f\in C^*$ because the action is bilinear; the same holds for $\rho(am)$ and $a\rho(m)$. Separation [F4] gives $\rho(m+n)=\rho(m)+\rho(n)$ and $\rho(am)=a\rho(m)$, so $\rho$ is linear.

Suppose now $C$ is finite-dimensional, without using AC. By [F6] let $c_1,\dots,c_n$ be a finite ordered basis, with coordinate functionals $c_1^*,\dots,c_n^*$ from [F9]. For any $f\in C^*$, the functionals $f$ and $\sum_i f(c_i)c_i^*$ agree on every basis vector and hence on all of $C$. For a left $C^*$-module vector $m$, put $t_m=\sum_{i=1}^n(c_i^*\cdot m)\otimes c_i$. Then $(\operatorname{id}\otimes f)t_m=\sum_i f(c_i)(c_i^*\cdot m)=f\cdot m$, so every module vector is rational. Any tensor in $M\otimes C$ can be re-expanded as $\sum_i y_i\otimes c_i$, and evaluating against $c_j^*$ recovers $y_j$; therefore the representing tensor is unique. This finite-coordinate argument uses no basis extension or arbitrary choice.

Suppose now $C$ is finite-dimensional, without using AC. Let $c_1,\dots,c_n$ be a finite ordered basis with dual basis $c_1^*,\dots,c_n^*$ by [F8]. For any left $C^*$-module vector $m$, put $t_m=\sum_{i=1}^n(c_i^*\cdot m)\otimes c_i$. For $f=\sum_i f(c_i)c_i^*$, one has $(\operatorname{id}\otimes f)t_m=\sum_i f(c_i)(c_i^*\cdot m)=f\cdot m$, so every module vector is rational. The representing tensor is unique because the dual basis coordinates recover its first-factor coefficients. This finite-coordinate argument uses no basis extension or arbitrary choice.

Now let $M$ be a rational left $C^*$-module. For each $m$, existence in [F3] and separation in step 1.3 make its representing tensor unique in the applicable branch; define $\rho(m)$ to be that unique tensor. Unique existence defines this function without an additional choice. For $m,n$ and $a\in k$, the tensors $\rho(m+n)$ and $\rho(m)+\rho(n)$ have the same evaluation under every $f\in C^*$ because the action is bilinear; the same holds for $\rho(am)$ and $a\rho(m)$. The separation proved in step 1.3 gives $\rho(m+n)=\rho(m)+\rho(n)$ and $\rho(am)=a\rho(m)$, so $\rho$ is linear.

Fix $m$ and write $\rho(m)=\sum_i m_i\otimes c_i$. Set $T=(\rho\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho(m)-(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta)\rho(m)\in M\otimes C\otimes C$. For any $f,g\in C^*$, evaluation of the first term by $\operatorname{id}_M\otimes f\otimes g$ is $\sum_i g(c_i)(f\cdot m_i)=f\cdot(g\cdot m)$, while evaluation of the second term is $\sum_i(f*g)(c_i)m_i=(f*g)\cdot m$. The module associativity law makes these equal. Hence every such pairing annihilates $T$. For fixed $g$, the tensor $(\operatorname{id}_{M\otimes C}\otimes g)(T)\in M\otimes C$ is annihilated by every $\operatorname{id}_M\otimes f$, so it is zero by [A1] and [F4]. Since this holds for every $g$, a second application of [F4] to the last $C$ factor gives $T=0$. Thus $\rho$ is coassociative.

Fix $m$ and write $\rho(m)=\sum_i m_i\otimes c_i$. Set $T=(\rho\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho(m)-(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta)\rho(m)\in M\otimes C\otimes C$. For any $f,g\in C^*$, evaluation of the first term by $\operatorname{id}_M\otimes f\otimes g$ is $\sum_i g(c_i)(f\cdot m_i)=f\cdot(g\cdot m)$, while evaluation of the second term is $\sum_i(f*g)(c_i)m_i=(f*g)\cdot m$. The module associativity law makes these equal. Hence every such pairing annihilates $T$. For fixed $g$, the tensor $(\operatorname{id}_{M\otimes C}\otimes g)(T)\in M\otimes C$ is annihilated by every $\operatorname{id}_M\otimes f$, so it is zero by the separation in step 1.3. Since this holds for every $g$, a second application of that separation result to the last $C$ factor gives $T=0$. Thus $\rho$ is coassociative.

If $u:M\to N$ is a comodule map, then $f\cdot u(m)=(\operatorname{id}_N\otimes f)\rho_N(u(m))=(\operatorname{id}_N\otimes f)(u\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M(m)=u(f\cdot m)$ for every $f,m$, so $u$ is a module map. Conversely, if $u$ is a module map, then $(\operatorname{id}_N\otimes f)(\rho_N(u(m))-(u\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M(m))=f\cdot u(m)-u(f\cdot m)=0$ for every $f$. The difference is a finite tensor in $N\otimes C$, so [A1] and [F4] make it zero. Hence $u$ is a comodule map.

If $u:M\to N$ is a comodule map, then $f\cdot u(m)=(\operatorname{id}_N\otimes f)\rho_N(u(m))=(\operatorname{id}_N\otimes f)(u\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M(m)=u(f\cdot m)$ for every $f,m$, so $u$ is a module map. Conversely, if $u$ is a module map, then $(\operatorname{id}_N\otimes f)(\rho_N(u(m))-(u\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M(m))=f\cdot u(m)-u(f\cdot m)=0$ for every $f$. The difference is a finite tensor in $N\otimes C$, so the separation in step 1.3 makes it zero. Hence $u$ is a comodule map.

In the finite-dimensional case, every finite tensor in $X\otimes C$ has a unique expansion $\sum_i x_i\otimes c_i$, and evaluating against each $c_i^*$ recovers $x_i$. Every finite tensor in $X\otimes C\otimes C$ likewise has an expansion $\sum_{i,j}x_{ij}\otimes c_i\otimes c_j$, and evaluations against $c_i^*\otimes c_j^*$ recover all coefficients. Therefore the separation uses in steps 1.3, 1.4, 2.2, and 2.3 can all be carried out without AC when $C$ is finite-dimensional. Together with step 1.5, this proves the full object and morphism correspondence in that branch without AC.

In the finite-dimensional case, re-expanding the second factors of any finite tensor in a basis $c_1,\dots,c_n$ gives $\sum_i x_i\otimes c_i$, and evaluation against $c_i^*$ recovers each $x_i$. For a tensor in $X\otimes C\otimes C$, re-expand both $C$ factors to obtain $\sum_{i,j}x_{ij}\otimes c_i\otimes c_j$; evaluations against $c_i^*$ and $c_j^*$ recover every coefficient. These finite-coordinate arguments are exactly the choice-free separation branch established in step 1.3, so the separation uses in steps 2.1, 3.2, and 3.3 need no AC when $C$ is finite-dimensional. Together with step 1.4, this proves the full object and morphism correspondence in that branch without AC.

Steps 1.1–1.3 construct a rational module from every right comodule and recover its unique original coaction; steps 1.4, 2.1, and 2.2 construct a right coaction from every rational module; step 2.3 proves the correspondence on maps. Steps 1.5 and 3.1 prove the full correspondence without AC when $C$ is finite-dimensional.

Steps 1.1–1.3 construct a rational module from every right comodule and recover its unique original coaction; steps 2.1, 3.1, and 3.2 construct a right coaction from every rational module; step 3.3 proves the correspondence on maps. Steps 1.4 and 4.1 prove the full correspondence without AC when $C$ is finite-dimensional.

Let $\theta_{A,A}:A^*\otimes A^*\to(A\otimes A)^*$ be the isomorphism in [F3]. Define
 $\Delta_{A^*}:=\theta_{A,A}^{-1}\circ m_A^*$ and $\varepsilon_{A^*}(f):=f(1_A)$.
For $f\in A^*$ and $a,b\in A$, evaluation through $\theta_{A,A}$ gives $\theta_{A,A}(\Delta_{A^*}f)(a\otimes b)=f(ab)$.
The tensor-product pairing on three finite-dimensional factors, obtained by applying [F3] twice and reassociating, separates elements of $A^*\otimes A^*\otimes A^*$.

Let $\theta_{A,A}:A^*\otimes A^*\to(A\otimes A)^*$ be the isomorphism in [F3], applicable because $A$ is finite-dimensional and therefore has a finite basis by [F6]. Define
 $\Delta_{A^*}:=\theta_{A,A}^{-1}\circ m_A^*$ and $\varepsilon_{A^*}(f):=f(1_A)$.
For $f\in A^*$ and $a,b\in A$, evaluation through $\theta_{A,A}$ gives $\theta_{A,A}(\Delta_{A^*}f)(a\otimes b)=f(ab)$.
The tensor-product pairing on three finite-dimensional factors, obtained by applying [F3] twice and reassociating, separates elements of $A^*\otimes A^*\otimes A^*$.

For finite-dimensional coalgebra $C$, define $\eta_C:C\to C^{**}$ by $\eta_C(c)(f)=f(c)$. A finite basis of $C$ and its dual show $\eta_C$ is a vector-space isomorphism. For $f,g\in C^*$, evaluating $\Delta_{C^{**}}\eta_C(c)$ against $f\otimes g$ gives $\eta_C(c)(f*g)=(f*g)(c)=(f\otimes g)(\Delta_C(c))$. The same evaluation of $(\eta_C\otimes\eta_C)\Delta_C(c)$ has that value; finite tensor duality [F3] therefore gives equality of the coproducts. Also $\varepsilon_{C^{**}}(\eta_C(c))=\eta_C(c)(\varepsilon_C)=\varepsilon_C(c)$. Hence $\eta_C$ is a coalgebra isomorphism.

For finite-dimensional coalgebra $C$, [F6] gives a finite basis of $C$; define $\eta_C:C\to C^{**}$ by $\eta_C(c)(f)=f(c)$. A finite basis of $C$ and its dual show $\eta_C$ is a vector-space isomorphism. For $f,g\in C^*$, evaluating $\Delta_{C^{**}}\eta_C(c)$ against $f\otimes g$ gives $\eta_C(c)(f*g)=(f*g)(c)=(f\otimes g)(\Delta_C(c))$. The same evaluation of $(\eta_C\otimes\eta_C)\Delta_C(c)$ has that value; finite tensor duality [F3] therefore gives equality of the coproducts. Also $\varepsilon_{C^{**}}(\eta_C(c))=\eta_C(c)(\varepsilon_C)=\varepsilon_C(c)$. Hence $\eta_C$ is a coalgebra isomorphism.

Let $\phi:A\to B$ be a unital algebra map between finite-dimensional algebras. Its transpose $\phi^*:B^*\to A^*$ preserves counits since $\varepsilon_{A^*}(\phi^*f)=f(\phi(1_A))=f(1_B)=\varepsilon_{B^*}(f)$. For $a,a'\in A$, evaluation of $\Delta_{A^*}(\phi^*f)$ at $a\otimes a'$ is $f(\phi(aa'))=f(\phi(a)\phi(a'))$. Writing $\Delta_{B^*}(f)=\sum_r f_r\otimes g_r$, evaluation of $(\phi^*\otimes\phi^*)\Delta_{B^*}(f)$ at $a\otimes a'$ is $\sum_r f_r(\phi(a))g_r(\phi(a'))=\Delta_{B^*}(f)(\phi(a)\otimes\phi(a'))=f(\phi(a)\phi(a'))$ by the defining transpose formula in 1.1. Since $A$ is finite-dimensional, [F3] separates the tensors, so $\phi^*$ is a coalgebra map.

Let $\phi:A\to B$ be a unital algebra map between finite-dimensional algebras, so [F6] supplies finite bases for both. Its transpose $\phi^*:B^*\to A^*$ preserves counits since $\varepsilon_{A^*}(\phi^*f)=f(\phi(1_A))=f(1_B)=\varepsilon_{B^*}(f)$. For $a,a'\in A$, evaluation of $\Delta_{A^*}(\phi^*f)$ at $a\otimes a'$ is $f(\phi(aa'))=f(\phi(a)\phi(a'))$. Writing $\Delta_{B^*}(f)=\sum_r f_r\otimes g_r$, evaluation of $(\phi^*\otimes\phi^*)\Delta_{B^*}(f)$ at $a\otimes a'$ is $\sum_r f_r(\phi(a))g_r(\phi(a'))=\Delta_{B^*}(f)(\phi(a)\otimes\phi(a'))=f(\phi(a)\phi(a'))$ by the defining transpose formula in 1.1. Since $A$ is finite-dimensional, [F3] separates the tensors, so $\phi^*$ is a coalgebra map.

For finite-dimensional $A$, define $\eta_A:A\to A^{**}$ by $\eta_A(a)(f)=f(a)$. If $a_1,\dots,a_n$ is a basis and $a_1^*,\dots,a_n^*$ its dual basis, then $\eta_A(a_i)$ is the dual basis to $a_i^*$; hence $\eta_A$ is a vector-space isomorphism. For $f\in A^*$, convolution in $A^{**}$ and the defining equation for $\Delta_{A^*}$ give $(\eta_A(a)*\eta_A(b))(f)=\sum \eta_A(a)(f_1)\eta_A(b)(f_2)=\Delta_{A^*}(f)(a\otimes b)=f(ab)=\eta_A(ab)(f)$. The unit of $A^{**}$ is the counit of $A^*$, and its value on $f$ is $f(1_A)=\eta_A(1_A)(f)$. Thus $\eta_A$ is an algebra isomorphism.

For finite-dimensional $A$, [F6] supplies a finite basis; define $\eta_A:A\to A^{**}$ by $\eta_A(a)(f)=f(a)$. If $a_1,\dots,a_n$ is a basis and $a_1^*,\dots,a_n^*$ its dual basis, then $\eta_A(a_i)$ is the dual basis to $a_i^*$; hence $\eta_A$ is a vector-space isomorphism. For $f\in A^*$, convolution in $A^{**}$ and the defining equation for $\Delta_{A^*}$ give $(\eta_A(a)*\eta_A(b))(f)=\sum \eta_A(a)(f_1)\eta_A(b)(f_2)=\Delta_{A^*}(f)(a\otimes b)=f(ab)=\eta_A(ab)(f)$. The unit of $A^{**}$ is the counit of $A^*$, and its value on $f$ is $f(1_A)=\eta_A(1_A)(f)$. Thus $\eta_A$ is an algebra isomorphism.

value.quote:
$V$ is **infinite-dimensional over $F$** when it is not finite-dimensional over
$F$, that is, when $V$ has **no** finite basis. No number is attached to such a
space here: the symbol $\dim_F V$ is defined only in the finite-dimensional case,
and the expression $\dim_F V = \infty$ is not used.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and suppose
$V$ has a spanning subset $S$ ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]) with
$S \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]). Then:

1. every linearly independent subset $L \subseteq V$
   ([[def-linear-independence]]) is finite ([[def-countable]]), and the unique
   $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $L \approx m$ satisfies $m \le n$;
2. no linearly independent subset of $V$ is equinumerous with $\mathbb{N}$.

value: A functional $f\in C^*$ is determined by the sequence $a_n=f(e_n)$, and every sequence occurs: for a finite-support vector $\sum_n\lambda_ne_n$, define $f(\sum_n\lambda_ne_n)=\sum_n\lambda_na_n$. The convolution satisfies $(f*g)(e_n)=f(e_n)g(e_n)$, so under this identification $C^*$ is the pointwise algebra $k^{\mathbb N}$ with unit $\varepsilon=(1,1,\ldots)$. The coordinate indicator functionals $\delta_n$ are linearly independent, hence $C^*$ is infinite-dimensional.

A functional $f\in C^*$ is determined by the sequence $a_n=f(e_n)$, and every sequence occurs: for a finite-support vector $\sum_n\lambda_ne_n$, define $f(\sum_n\lambda_ne_n)=\sum_n\lambda_na_n$. The convolution satisfies $(f*g)(e_n)=f(e_n)g(e_n)$, so under this identification $C^*$ is the pointwise algebra $k^{\mathbb N}$ with unit $\varepsilon=(1,1,\ldots)$. The basis vectors $e_n$ are linearly independent in $C$, and the coordinate functionals $\delta_n$ are linearly independent in $C^*$ because evaluating a finite linear relation at $e_j$ recovers its $j$th coefficient. Both independent sets are equinumerous with $\mathbb N$. By [F6], neither $C$ nor $C^*$ has a finite spanning set, hence neither has a finite basis; both are infinite-dimensional by [F6].

value.quote:
Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$
